The '''root test''' tests the convergence of the [[number sequence#Partial_sum|partial sum sequence]] of an infinite [[number sequence]].

$$
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}
\begin{cases}
>1 \Rightarrow (S_n) \text{ diverges,}\\
< 1 \Rightarrow (S_n) \text{ converges,}\\
=1 \Rightarrow (S_n) \text{ diverges or converges (test inconclusive).}\\
\end{cases}
$$
<ref>{{#cite:Q2449}}</ref>

{{Hidden example}}

$$
a_n=
\begin{cases}
2^{-n}, & n \text{ even},\\
3^{-n}, & n \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
$$

'''Q''': Does $(S_n)$ converge?

'''Solution''':

$n \to \infty$, $\sqrt[n]{a_n}$ alternates between $1/2$ and $1/3$.

Hence $\nexists \lim\sqrt[n]{a_n}$, but

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}=\frac{1}{2}<1,
$$

So by the root test, $(S_n)$ does converge.

{{End hidden}}

{{Hidden proof}}

'''When''' $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}>1$:

Choose arbitrary $q \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.

$$
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}>q>1 \\
\Rightarrow
\limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n|>\lim_{n \to \infty} q^n>1 \\
\because \lim_{n \to \infty} q^n = \infty \\
\therefore  \limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n| = \infty
$$

so $(S_n)$ must diverge.

'''When''' $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}<1$:

Choose arbitrary $q \in \mathbb{R}$ s.t.

$$
\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{[a_n]} < q < 1
$$

then

$$
\limsup_{n \to \infty} |a_n| < \lim_{n \to \infty} q^n \\
\Rightarrow \lim_{n \to \infty} -(q^n) < \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n < \lim_{n \to \infty} q^n \\
\because \limsup_{n \to \infty} (-q^n) = 0 = \lim_{n \to \infty} q^n \\
\therefore  \limsup_{n \to \infty} a_n = 0
$$
by [[squeeze theorem]].

so $(S_n)$ must converge.

{{End hidden}}
